papers.title: The Fat-Body Secreted Neuropeptide CCHa2 Signals Insulin-Producing Cells in the Brain to Promote Sleep.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental behavior regulated by diverse environmental and physiological cues. While the central mechanisms underlying sleep regulation have been investigated in detail, far less is known about how nutrient signals from the periphery are communicated to the brain to modulate sleep. Here, we perform a targeted RNAi screen of genes enriched in the fat body and regulated by feeding state to identify genes that function in the fat body to regulate sleep in Drosophila. This analysis found that fat body-specific knockdown of CCHa2 significantly reduced sleep duration and sleep depth in fed flies, phenocopying sleep in starved flies. CCHa2-deficient flies exhibited reduced glycogen stores and diminished feeding drive. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomic atlases confirms that the CCHa2 receptor (CCHa2-R) is selectively expressed in insulin-producing cells (IPCs) of the fly brain. We find that knockdown of CCHa2-R in IPCs recapitulates the sleep loss phenotype of CCHa2 mutants, supporting a role in adipose-brain signaling. Further screening of genes identified in single cell atlases as being enriched in IPCs led to the identification of numerous genes that function in IPCs to regulate sleep, including modulators of wnt and insulin signaling. Together, these findings identify a fat body-IPC axis that is a critical modulator of sleep duration and intensity.

papers.title: Sleep Renormalizes Negative Emotional Generalization
papers.abstract: Overgeneralization of negative experiences co-occurs with sleep disruption and characterizes anxiety and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A strategically-designed behavioral paradigm tested whether sleep shifts emotional generalization away from negative and toward positive representations. Participants learned positive, negative, or neutral face-outcome associations, then completed immediate and delayed generalization testing with morphed faces after sleep or wakefulness. Sleep selectively enhanced positive generalization, whereas wakefulness favored negative generalization. To uncover the underlying neural mechanisms, individual variability in generalization was examined using fMRI and high-density EEG. Amygdala and limbic activity during outcome-processing predicted both stronger immediate negative generalization and a sleep-specific shift toward positive generalization. Additionally, sleep-spindle activity positively correlated with post-sleep increases in positive generalization and reductions in negative generalization. Together, these findings identify a neural mechanism through which sleep reduces negative bias while strengthening positive representations, highlighting a pathway by which sleep may protect against maladaptive generalization associated with anxiety and PTSD.

papers.title: Simvastatin Modulates Astrocyte and Microglial Reactivity and Aggressive Behavior After Chronic Sleep Deprivation in Rats.
papers.abstract: Chronic sleep deprivation (SD) disrupts central nervous system homeostasis, promoting behavioral alterations and glial remodeling within limbic structures. Although simvastatin exhibits pleiotropic effects, its influence on astrocytic and microglial responses during prolonged sleep loss remains poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of SD and simvastatin on behavior, systemic inflammatory mediators, and glial reactivity in the dorsal hippocampus (HPC) and amygdala (AMY). Sixty male Wistar rats (~75 days old; n = 15/group) were assigned to Control (CG), Sleep Deprived (SD), Simvastatin 4.2 mg/kg (SIM4.2), or Simvastatin 20 mg/kg (SIM20) groups. Animals underwent the modified multiple platform method (18 h/day) for 45 consecutive days, with daily oral simvastatin administration. Social behavior was assessed using the resident-intruder test, circulating cytokines by ELISA, and glial responses by GFAP and IBA-1 immunohistochemistry, including microglial morphological classification (Types I-III). SD increased aggressive/reactive behavior and astrocytic and microglial reactivity in the dorsal HPC, accompanied by a shift from homeostatic (Type I) toward reactive (Types II and III) microglial phenotypes. Simvastatin attenuated these glial alterations, restoring a more homeostatic microglial profile and increasing non-social exploratory behavior. In contrast, glial alterations in the AMY were comparatively limited, indicating region-specific susceptibility to SD. Peripheral cytokine analysis revealed selective immunomodulatory effects, including reduced TGF-β and increased IL-8 in SIM20, whereas TNF-α and IL-6 remained unchanged. Overall, simvastatin modulated behavioral, systemic inflammatory, and glial responses to SD, supporting its pleiotropic effects and highlighting region-specific glial remodeling as a potential target for mitigating the consequences of chronic sleep loss.

papers.title: Sleep and Cardiometabolic Disease: A Wearable-Electronic Health Record Study in the US All of Us Research Program.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep health spans duration, quality, regularity, and timing, yet Life's Essential 8 scores sleep by duration alone, and regularity studies used about 1 week of data. How these dimensions, measured over months, relate to incident cardiometabolic disease is unknown, as is whether nightly sleep-cycle structure adds information. Methods: This cohort study included US adults in the All of Us Research Program with linked Fitbit and electronic health records (2009-2023). We derived 11 sleep metrics over a 180-day baseline (≥90 valid nights). Incident diagnoses, grouped into phecodes, were counted after a 180-day washout to limit reverse causation. Primary analyses related these metrics to prespecified endpoints, including a CVD composite (myocardial infarction, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, or ischemic stroke), heart failure, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Cox models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and comorbidity factors. Exploratory analyses examined wearable-estimated sleep cycles (7,199 participants; 1,017,812 sleep-stage nights). Results: Among 10,362 participants (median age, 53 years; 70% female), 230 developed the CVD composite (median follow-up, 3.7 years). Each 1-SD (29-minute) higher night-to-night variability in sleep duration was associated with higher CVD composite risk (hazard ratio, 1.24 [95% CI, 1.09-1.41]), as was higher variability in bedtime (1.23 [1.10-1.37]), waketime (1.20 [1.09-1.32]), and midpoint (1.21 [1.09-1.35]); mean sleep duration was not (0.96 [0.85-1.08]). Variability in sleep duration was also associated with heart failure (1.32 [1.13-1.55]), hypertension (1.16 [1.08-1.25]), and type 2 diabetes (1.20 [1.07-1.35]). More sleep cycles were associated with lower atrial arrhythmia risk (0.72 [0.58-0.89]), independent of sleep duration, regularity, and timing (0.58 [0.44-0.77]). Conclusions: Night-to-night irregularity in sleep duration and timing was associated with the CVD composite, heart failure, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes; mean duration was not associated with the CVD composite. More wearable-estimated sleep cycles were associated with lower atrial arrhythmia risk beyond conventional sleep metrics, a novel finding requiring confirmation.

papers.title: Novel sleep scoring method for neurodegenerative diseases: feasibility and reliability in advanced Parkinson disease.
papers.abstract: In neurodegenerative diseases, damage to sleep-wake regulating brain regions alters sleep architecture (e.g., loss of spindles and K-complexes, EEG slowing during wakefulness and REM sleep), challenging the current American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) rules for scoring sleep. In Parkinson disease (PD) patients, we assessed the feasibility and interrater reliability of a previously described novel sleep scoring methodology. Video-polysomnography of 15 PD patients and five age-matched controls were scored blinded by five trained raters (two neurologists and three technicians) with different levels of expertise. Recordings were first scored empirically following the AASM methodology and, when necessary, scored again using the following additional abnormal stages: abnormal Wake, Subwake, Undifferentiated NREM (UNREM) sleep, Poorly Structured N2 sleep, and abnormal REM sleep. Sleep microstructure alterations (e.g., encapsulated REM sleep behavior disorder) were also evaluated. The novel scoring method showed substantial interrater agreement (kappa = 0.75), comparable to the AASM method (kappa = 0.73). UNREM sleep was identified in 12 patients, Subwake in nine, and abnormal Wake, encapsulated REM sleep behavior disorder and abnormal REM sleep in seven. No abnormal stages were observed in three early PD patients or in any control. The presence of the abnormal sleep stages was associated with ageing and advanced PD with cognitive impairment and motor fluctuations. The novel sleep scoring methodology, which includes abnormal wakefulness as well as NREM and REM sleep stages, is feasible, reliable, and applicable in clinical practice for advanced PD patients undergoing video-polysomnography.

papers.title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.

papers.title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
papers.abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.

papers.title: Respiratory self-similarity is a sleep apnea endotype that predicts cardiovascular disease related mortality.
papers.abstract: Pathological respiratory chemoreflex activation (high loop gain) in sleep apnea may activate the carotid body and induce excessive sympathetic nerve output, and independently add to the risk of adverse outcomes. This study aims to determine whether a high loop gain of the respiratory control system during sleep, estimated by respiratory self-similarity (SS) and the algorithm-derived central respiratory event index (CREI), is associated with new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD-related mortality. A secondary analysis of The Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). High SS% and CREI were defined as the highest quartile. Lasso regression and restricted cubic spline assessed the relationship between SS%, CREI and CVD, CVD-mortality and all-cause mortality. A cumulative incidence function and a Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard model were used to evaluate this outcome accounting for competing risks. In adjusted models with age as a categorical variable divided by 65 years old, the highest quartile of SS% (HR 1.693, p: 0.017 in MESA and HR 1.240, p : 0.009 in SHHS) was associated with the incidence of CVD and was more prominent in males. A positive relationship between SS% (MESA: HR 1.429, p: 0.039; SHHS HR1.176, p:0.018 ) for the continuous metrics and CVD mortality in both cohorts was more apparent in men than in women. The categorical high-exposure association with CVD mortality was not consistent across cohorts.The associations were significantly attenuated when adjusted by age as a continuous metric. An endotype of sleep apnea reflecting high loop gain is associated with CVD and CVD mortality, especially in males.

papers.title: High-frequency EEG activity moderates the association between amyloid burden and tau in cognitively normal adults
papers.abstract: Background: Resting electroencephalogram (EEG) may capture early excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) imbalance in Alzheimer's disease, but its relationship to beta-amyloid and tau in cognitively normal adults is unclear. Methods: We analyzed resting-state EEG from 24 older adults, 21 cognitively normal (13 beta-amyloid-negative, 8 beta-amyloid-positive) and 3 with MCI/AD (all beta-amyloid-positive), with beta-amyloid positron emission tomography (PET); 20 of the cognitively normal adults also had tau PET. Four parietal measures related to E-I balance and excitability (periodic gamma power, alpha-gamma and theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling [PAC], and the aperiodic exponent) were related to beta-amyloid burden and to early medial temporal lobe (MTL) tau, adjusting for age and sex. Results: In 21 cognitively normal adults, higher beta-amyloid burden was associated with higher parietal periodic gamma power (beta= +0.50, p = 0.025). No E-I measure was associated with MTL tau across all participants. However, in beta-amyloid-positive adults, higher periodic gamma was associated with higher MTL tau, most strongly in the entorhinal cortex (beta = +0.90, p = 0.002), with no association in beta-amyloid-negative adults. Importantly, periodic gamma also moderated the association between beta-amyloid and MTL tau (p = 0.012; consistent across MTL regions after FDR correction). Conclusions: In this pilot study, parietal periodic gamma, an EEG marker of cortical excitability, increased with beta-amyloid burden and was related to MTL tau only in the presence of beta-amyloid. Periodic gamma is a candidate marker of beta-amyloid-related E-I imbalance that warrants confirmation in larger samples.

papers.title: Sleep architecture disruption and coordinated patterns of inflammatory and extracellular matrix biomarkers in obstructive sleep apnea: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the associations between circulating inflammatory, extracellular matrix (ECM), and oxidative stress biomarkers and polysomnographic parameters across different severity levels of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), with adjustment for body mass index (BMI). Seventy adults with confirmed OSA were categorized as mild-to-moderate or severe based on apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). Serum levels of TNF-α, IL-6, MMP-2, MMP-9, desmosine, cellular fibronectin (cFN), syndecan-1 (SDC-1), glutathione (GSH), and malondialdehyde (MDA) were measured using ELISA or spectrophotometric methods. Biomarker concentrations were natural-log transformed to satisfy normality assumptions; between-group comparisons were adjusted for BMI using ANCOVA. Associations among biomarkers and clinical variables were assessed using Spearman correlation, BMI-adjusted partial correlation, and network analysis. Severe OSA was associated with higher levels of TNF-α, IL-6, MMP-2, MMP-9, desmosine, and cFN compared with mild-to-moderate OSA (all p < 0.05). SDC-1 reached statistical significance after BMI adjustment (p = 0.009). These biomarkers were positively associated with AHI, oxygen desaturation index (ODI), desaturation count, and time spent with SpO₂ <90% (T90), and inversely associated with N3 sleep duration. After adjustment for BMI, strong inter-biomarker partial correlations (r = 0.831-0.921, p < 0.001) formed a densely connected inflammatory-ECM cluster; this pattern remained significant, albeit more modest in magnitude, in sensitivity analyses using unadjusted Spearman correlations (ρ = 0.427-0.655, p < 0.001). GSH and MDA showed weaker and more isolated associations. OSA severity is associated with coordinated patterns among inflammatory and ECM-related biomarkers that parallel hypoxic burden and sleep architecture changes. In contrast, systemic oxidative stress markers appear less integrated within these patterns. These findings support the potential utility of multi-biomarker approaches in reflecting disease-related physiological alterations, potentially arising from both systemic and local upper airway tissue processes.

papers.title: Diagnostic value of extending outpatient EEG to record sleep - A retrospective study.
papers.abstract: Evidence for the utility of sleep electroencephalography (EEG) in the diagnosis of epilepsy is inconsistent, often necessitating repeat visits and sleep deprivation (SD), which increases patient and resource burden. In our setting in India, patients are often referred for EEG immediately following consultation (single visit) and EEG sessions are extended to allow for spontaneous sleep acquisition without prior SD. We aimed to evaluate the success rate of achieving sleep during these extended outpatient recordings and its incremental diagnostic yield for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). We retrospectively analyzed 1762 outpatient EEGs from patients (45% female) with suspected or known epilepsy. All patients underwent an extended routine EEG (~40-50 min), incorporating standard activation procedures and aiming to capture spontaneous sleep where possible. Successful sleep acquisition was defined as the attainment of at least NREM stage N2. IED detection rates were compared between wakefulness and sleep across different epilepsy types. Sleep was achieved in 70.5% of patients (median age, 28 years; IQR: 16-55; range, 0.3-90). The proportion attaining sleep increased with recording duration, from 36.7% at 20 min to 55.6% at 30 min and 66.7% at 50 min, with a median time to sleep onset of 20 min. Among 1199 patients with both awake and sleep states captured, wakefulness identified IEDs in 29% (n = 350), while sleep captured unique IEDs in an additional 12% (n = 141), increasing the total yield significantly. In a sub-analysis of confirmed epilepsy cases (n = 751), wakefulness showed IEDs in 42% (n = 315), with sleep adding another 16% (n = 123). The diagnostic yield of sleep recordings was significantly higher than that of wakefulness alone (OR: 1.31; 95% CI: 1.02-1.68; p = 0.043), particularly among adults with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) (OR: 2.20; 95% CI: 1.30-3.73; p = 0.004) and children with self-limited epilepsy (OR: ∞; p = 0.031). Despite a busy outpatient setting, 70.5% of patients attained N2 sleep during an extended EEG recording without SD. Sleep capture increased progressively with recording duration, with the greatest incremental gain between 20 and 30 min, suggesting that a modest extension beyond 20 min substantially increases the likelihood of capturing sleep. Sleep recording increased IED detection over wakefulness alone, particularly in children, in adults with IGE, and in self-limited epilepsies. Whether this approach can substitute for a sleep-deprived EEG requires prospective, head-to-head evaluation.

papers.title: Exercise and physiological monitoring in isolated, confined and extreme environments and space analogues: A scoping review.
papers.abstract: This scoping review synthesized evidence on physical activity/exercise and physiological monitoring in isolated, confined and extreme (ICE) environments, with emphasis on Antarctic missions and space analogues. ICE exposures combine cold stress, confinement, disrupted light-dark cycles and psychosocial strain, which can challenge musculoskeletal integrity, cardiovascular regulation, sleep/circadian function and cognition. Following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched Web of Science, Embase, Scopus and PubMed/Medline, complemented by grey literature and AI-assisted citation chasing. Eligible reports included human studies in ICE/analogue settings that implemented or quantified physical activity/exercise and/or physiological monitoring. Seventeen studies published between 2003 and 2025 met inclusion criteria and were mapped across ICE characteristics, exercise protocols, monitoring technologies, outcomes and research gaps. Exercise was reported as a potential countermeasure to attenuate selected aspects of deconditioning and support sleep and psychophysiological adaptation, particularly in bed rest and simulated confinement studies. Antarctic field studies more often characterized spontaneous physical activity, sleep/activity rhythms and field-adapted monitoring. Assessment strategies varied, ranging from self-reported logs and actigraphy in operational field settings to laboratory-grade measures in bed rest and simulated confinement studies. Overall, exercise emerged as a pragmatic, domain-specific countermeasure against deconditioning in ICE settings, with effectiveness varying by modality and physiological target. However, heterogeneity in exposure characterization, exercise dose and monitoring methods, despite feasible wearable-based capture of behavioural and physiological signals, limited comparability and mechanistic inference. Future ICE research should prioritize harmonized reporting, standardized monitoring and longitudinal designs linking exercise exposure to physiological, behavioural and operational outcomes.

papers.title: The relevance of sleep and chronopsychology in understanding maladaptive behaviors in eating disorders: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and sleep-wake dysregulation have been increasingly linked to psychiatric conditions, yet their role in eating disorders and addiction-like maladaptive behaviors remains insufficiently examined in an integrative framework. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on chronotype, circadian misalignment, sleep features, and behavioral addictions across anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, orthorexic tendencies, and night eating syndrome. Literature published between 1970 and 2025 was identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, and reference screening, focusing on chronobiological, sleep-related, neuroendocrine, and behavioral aspects of eating disorders. Delayed sleep timing, eveningness preference, and insomnia symptoms commonly co-occur with disordered eating. Findings suggest overlapping mechanisms linking circadian dysregulation, sleep-related and compulsive, reward-driven behaviors, including binge eating and compensatory practices. Objective measures indicate alterations in sleep continuity, slow-wave sleep, and REM parameters. Neuroendocrine evidence further supports links among biological rhythms, appetite regulation, and sleep regulation. Preliminary chronotherapeutic interventions, such as light exposure and sleep phase modification, show promise but remain insufficiently tested. Overall, subclinical, clinical and emerging eating disorders remain underrepresented in chronobiological research. Circadian misalignment may represent a clinically relevant and modifiable dimension underlying maladaptive eating behaviors. However, fragmented evidence and methodological limitations restrict firm conclusions. A structured research agenda is proposed to guide future integrative research.

papers.title: Adjunctive perampanel in children with focal-onset seizures and developmental delay or intellectual disability: efficacy, tolerability, and sleep benefits.
papers.abstract: Perampanel (PER), a noncompetitive alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor antagonist, is used to treat focal-onset seizures in patients aged ≥4 years. However, evidence in children with focal-onset seizures and developmental delay (DD) and/or intellectual disability (ID) remains limited, particularly regarding sleep-related outcomes. This study evaluated the efficacy and tolerability of adjunctive PER in this population. This retrospective single-cohort study assessed the effectiveness of adjunctive PER for overall and sleep-related seizures and sleep disturbance, as well as tolerability based on adverse events and treatment retention, in patients aged <18 years with focal-onset seizures and DD/ID treated from January 2020 through December 2025. Among 83 screened patients, 57 who received PER for >3 months were included. Genetic etiology was most common (23/57, 40.4%), and 91.2% had drug-resistant epilepsy. Sleep-related seizures occurred in 73.7%, and sleep disturbance was present in 50.9%. Hypersomnolence (29.8%) and aggression (24.6%) were the most common adverse events, and 51 patients (89.5%) remained on PER for ≥12 months. Overall responder rates (≥50% seizure reduction) at 3, 6, and 12 months were 89.5% (51/57), 81.1% (43/53), and 74.5% (38/51), with seizure-free rates of 45.6%, 49.1%, and 43.1%, respectively. Corresponding responder rates for sleep-related seizures were 92.9%, 89.7%, and 76.9% (39/42, 35/39, and 30/39), with seizure-free rates of 40.5%, 46.2%, and 30.8%. Among 29 patients with preexisting sleep disturbance, 93.1% improved. Adjunctive PER demonstrated favorable effectiveness and tolerability in children with focal-onset seizures and DD/ID despite substantial drug resistance and was also associated with improvement in sleep disturbance.

papers.title: Diaphragm Weakness and Sleep-Related Breathing Disorders in Patients with Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathy.
papers.abstract: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) can cause respiratory muscle weakness, leading to diaphragm weakness (DW) and sleep-related breathing disorders (SRBD). We aimed to investigate clinical findings of DW and SRBD in patients with IIMs. In patients with biopsy-confirmed IIMs, demographics, respiratory symptoms, single-breath counting (SBC), arterial blood gas, upright/supine SpO2 and spirometry, diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO), maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressure (MIP, MEP), peak cough flow (PCF), and polysomnography parameters were prospectively evaluated. Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), STOP-BANG, and Mallampati scores were recorded. The presence of at least one of two findings was considered suggestive of DW: (1) paradoxical abdominal movement (PAM), (2) upright-supine forced vital capacity (FVC) difference of ≥20%. Sixteen patients (12 female/4 male, mean age: 54.4 ± 11.2/y, 9 dermatomyositis [DM], 6 polymyositis [PM], 1 inclusion body myositis [IBM]) were evaluated. Findings consistent with DW were observed in 25% of patients, and all of them had DM. MIP, MEP, and PCF were reduced in the majority of patients. Supine FVC% and supine SpO2 were significantly lower in patients with DW (P = .001 and P = .003, respectively). PaO2, SaO2, SBC, and PCF were lower, and the upright-supine SpO₂ difference was greater in patients with DW, although these differences were not statistically significant. Polysomnography was performed in 68.8% (n = 11) of patients. All 11 patients who underwent polysomnography had obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) (2 severe, 4 moderate, 5 mild). Findings suggestive of DW were observed in 25% of patients with IIM and exclusively in those with DM, while OSA was identified in all patients who underwent polysomnography. These findings may support the clinical evaluation of both diaphragm involvement and sleep-related breathing disorders in patients with IIM.

papers.title: Autonomic Reactivity and EEG-defined Clusters Reveal Distinct Chronic Pain Profiles.
papers.abstract: This study examined whether integrating stress-related heart rate variability (HRV) with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) could characterize physiological subgroups in Chronic pain after spine surgery (CPSS). A total of 177 patients completed pain- and emotion-related questionnaires, a 3-minute resting-state EEG recording, and HRV assessments during baseline, mental arithmetic stress, and recovery. Participants were grouped by the direction of stress-related low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio change. Principal component analysis and unsupervised clustering were applied to 437 EEG features encompassing absolute power, cerebral asymmetry, and theta/beta ratio (TBR). After multivariate outlier detection, 168 participants underwent clustering. A 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA examined HRV-group and EEG-cluster effects on pain scores. LF/HF -decreased group (n = 56) reported higher depressive symptom scores than the increase group (n = 121, P = 0.045), without significant pain differences. Among 437 EEG features, PC1 reflected beta activity (34.39% variance), PC2 frontal/frontotemporal asymmetry (14.52%), and PC3 TBR features (9.55%). Two EEG clusters (n = 88 and n = 80) showed no significant pain- or emotion-related differences. Factorial analysis revealed nonsignificant HRV (P = .056) and EEG main effects (P = .107), but a nominally significant interaction [P = .030, partial η² = .028 (HC3-robust P = .044)]. Within EEG Cluster 0, the LF/HF-decrease group reported higher pain scores than the LF/HF-increase group (70.9 vs. 42.3; Tukey-adjusted P = .019). Integrating HRV-EEG profiles may help characterize CPSS heterogeneity. These exploratory findings, without study-wide multiplicity adjustment, require independent validation before clinical application.

papers.title: DECAPPING PROTEIN 5 regulates the circadian clock in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: The Arabidopsis transcriptome must be continuously reshaped to integrate endogenous and environmental cues, including the circadian clock and ambient light. This reprogramming relies on the coordinated synthesis and degradation of mRNAs, yet the contribution of RNA decay factors to circadian regulation remains poorly characterized. Here, we show that nearly all core clock genes are high-amplitude clock-controlled genes (HA-CCGs). A meta-analysis of transcriptome-wide mRNA decay datasets revealed that HA-CCGs have consistently shorter half-lives across multiple studies. We further identify the mRNA decapping activator DECAPPING PROTEIN 5 (DCP5) as a key regulator of circadian RNA stability. Using iCLIP, we show that DCP5 binds preferentially to HA-CCG transcripts at AU-rich motifs in their 3' UTRs, thereby modulating their stability. Accordingly, the dcp5 mutant displays an extended circadian period at both physiological and molecular levels. Our findings establish mRNA decay as a post-transcriptional regulatory layer that fine-tunes the decay of multiple key transcripts within the circadian system.

papers.title: Wearable Evidence Linking Dyskinesia Burden to Sleep Quality in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances affect 60-80% of people with Parkinson's disease (PD) and worsen quality of life. Dyskinesia is a common complication of dopaminergic therapy, yet its link to sleep quality is poorly understood. To examine whether clinician-rated and objectively measured dyskinesia are associated with sleep quality in PD. We studied 47 people with PD (median age 68 years; 44.7% women; median disease duration 5 years). Sleep was measured with Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Dyskinesia was rated clinically (MDS-UPDRS items 4.1, 4.2) and objectively over 7 days using Parkinson's KinetiGraph (median dyskinesia score; DKS). Regression models adjusted for age, sex, motor severity, levodopa dose, and disease duration. All dyskinesia measures predicted poorer sleep unadjusted. After adjusting for levodopa dose, only DKS remained significant (B = 0.18, P = 0.047). Adding disease duration attenuated this (P = 0.051). Wearable-derived dyskinesia, but not clinician-rated dyskinesia, independently predicted poorer sleep, supporting wearable monitoring in PD.

papers.title: Probable Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder Associated With Escitalopram in a Patient With Schizoaffective Disorder: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia in which the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep is lost, and patients act out their dreams. Serotonergic antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a recognized trigger, but in psychiatric patients the nocturnal behaviors are easily attributed to stress or to the primary illness. We report the case of a 46-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, maintained on aripiprazole 15 mg daily, who was started on escitalopram 10 mg at bedtime (day one); the dose was reduced to 5 mg on day 77. Around day 430, about 14 months after starting escitalopram and while taking 5 mg, he began to walk in his sleep and act out his dreams, including punching movements and, on one occasion, walking while holding a clothing iron, with no recollection on waking. The episodes occurred late in the night, with his eyes closed, two to three times a month and were accompanied by sleep paralysis and daytime sleepiness. His mental status examination and routine blood tests were unremarkable. He declined polysomnography and brain imaging, so a diagnosis of probable RBD, possibly associated with escitalopram, was made on clinical grounds; a non-REM parasomnia could not be excluded. On day 616, escitalopram was stopped and clonazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime was started at the same time. The episodes had stopped by day 665. Clonazepam was discontinued on day 772, and at the latest follow-up on day 1962 there had been no recurrence. Because clonazepam was started when escitalopram was withdrawn, the improvement cannot be attributed to stopping escitalopram alone, although the absence of recurrence after clonazepam was discontinued supports a role for the antidepressant. Clinicians who prescribe serotonergic antidepressants should take a sleep history from patients and their bed partners, arrange polysomnography where it is available, and review the suspected drug.

papers.title: Eyes-open resting-state EEG microstate analysis using ratio-normalized parameters across four- and seven-class solutions in healthy controls, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: BackgroundResting-state EEG microstate analysis indexes large-scale network dynamics, yet the value of ratio-normalized temporal parameters under the eyes-open resting (EOR) condition remains unexplored across the cognitive decline continuum.ObjectiveTo examine whether ratio-normalized microstate parameters from four- and seven-class clustering solutions under EOR differentiate healthy controls (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD).MethodsOne hundred and eighty participants (HC, MCI, and AD; n = 60 each) were recruited from a hospital-based cohort in an elderly Korean population. Resting-state EEG recorded under EOR was analyzed using MICROSTATELAB in EEGLAB. Absolute temporal parameters (duration, occurrence, coverage) and ratio-normalized forms (relative duration, relative occurrence) were compared using ANCOVA with age as covariate, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons.ResultsIn the four-class solution, three parameters reached nominal significance, none surviving FDR correction across the full set of 20 tests: coverage of Microstate B (visual network; F(2176) = 3.561, p = 0.030), relative occurrence of Microstate B (F(2176) = 5.281, p = 0.006), and relative occurrence of Microstate E (executive network; F(2176) = 3.816, p = 0.024). MCI showed higher visual and lower executive microstate engagement than AD (p ≤ 0.023); no contrast involving HC was significant. Absolute occurrence parameters were non-significant whereas their ratio-normalized counterparts were significant. The seven-class solution yielded no corrected effects.ConclusionsRatio-normalized EOR microstate parameters distinguished MCI from AD through visual and executive network engagement, with small-to-moderate effects and HC intermediate. The four-class solution outperformed the seven-class solution, contrasting with eyes-closed reports. As these analyses were exploratory and did not survive correction, confirmation in independent cohorts is required.

papers.title: Ultrasonographic assessment of diaphragmatic functions in relation to obstructive sleep apnea severity.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects 9-38% of adults and is associated with intermittent hypoxia, sleep fragmentation, and increased cardiovascular risk. Although the diaphragm contributes 60-80% of ventilatory effort, diaphragmatic functional changes in OSA remain inadequately characterized. Diaphragmatic ultrasonography offers a noninvasive, bedside method for functional assessment, but evidence in OSA is limited. To evaluate diaphragmatic function using ultrasonography in patients evaluated for suspected OSA and to determine its association with disease severity. This prospective cross-sectional study included 62 patients evaluated for suspected OSA attending inpatient and outpatient services at a tertiary care center between January 2024 and April 2025. OSA severity was classified using polysomnography-derived Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) as per American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) guidelines. Blinded ultrasonographic assessment measured right and left hemidiaphragm thickness, thickening fraction, and diaphragmatic excursion. Statistical analysis included Spearman's correlation, Kruskal-Wallis test, ordinal logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. The mean age was 51 years, with male predominance (72.6%). Most participants were overweight or obese. The median AHI was 25.6 events/hour, and severe OSA was present in 41.9% of participants, while mild OSA constituted 37.1%, reflecting referral-based nature of the cohort. None of the enrolled patients had AHI < 5. Left diaphragmatic excursion showed a weak positive correlation with AHI (ρ = 0.274; P = 0.031) and a multivariable-adjusted association with OSA severity (OR 1.125; 95% CI 1.026-1.249; P = 0.017). For identifying moderate-to-severe OSA, diaphragmatic ultrasonography demonstrated an AUC of 0.72 (95% CI 0.59-0.85; P = 0.002), with 66.1% accuracy, 59.0% sensitivity, and 78.3% specificity. Diaphragmatic function assessed by ultrasonography is largely preserved in OSA, with left diaphragmatic excursion showing a multivariable-adjusted association with disease severity, these findings primarily reflect a mixed-severity population with a substantial proportion of mild OSA. Bedside diaphragmatic ultrasound may serve as an exploratory adjunct for OSA risk stratification, particularly in resource-limited settings, pending external validation.

papers.title: Neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia: a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) is the standard of care for moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy (NE). Although some centers consider TH for mild NE, neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants who do not meet eligibility criteria are incompletely defined. Infants evaluated for TH based on perinatal risk factors, but who did not meet institutional eligibility criteria, were prospectively enrolled. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed at 24 months. Bayley-4 scores <85 were classified as sub-normative performance. Of 39 infants enrolled, 26 completed Bayley-4 assessments. Thirteen (50%) demonstrated sub-normative performance in at least one developmental domain; only one of them had an acute brain injury on MRI. Compared with infants with average-range performance, those with sub-normative performance had higher postnatal base deficits (10.1 vs 6 mmol/L, p 0.04), higher postnatal lactate levels (9.4 vs 4.9 mmol/L, p 0.05), and a trend toward less sleep-wake cycling on aEEG (45% vs 83%, p 0.06). A substantial proportion of infants evaluated for but not treated with TH demonstrated sub-normative developmental performance at 2 years. Absence of acute MRI-detected injury does not preclude later developmental vulnerability. These findings support longitudinal follow-up of infants who are evaluated for TH but do not meet TH criteria. Infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia demonstrated a measurable risk of neurodevelopmental vulnerability at 2 years, with 50% demonstrating sub-normative performance (>1 SD below the normative mean) in at least one domain on the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development Fourth Edition. Early postnatal metabolic abnormalities in infants evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia showed a potential association with later developmental outcomes. There is a need for improved risk stratification and structured longitudinal follow-up for infants evaluated for but who do not meet cooling criteria.

papers.title: Region-Adapted Multi-Nutrient Supplementation in Chinese Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A 12-Week Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Nutritional supplementation has produced inconsistent effects on autistic symptoms, and the evidence base is largely derived from Western populations. This study evaluated the preliminary efficacy and tolerability of a region-adapted multinutrient intervention in Chinese children with autism spectrum disorder. In this 12-wk pilot, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 50 children were assigned to receive either the intervention or a placebo. The primary endpoint was the change in the Autism Behavior Checklist total score. Secondary outcomes included developmental functioning assessed using the Psychoeducational Profile, Third Edition; gastrointestinal symptoms assessed using the Gastrointestinal Severity Index; and sleep assessed with the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire. Between-group differences were analysed using baseline-adjusted models. All participants completed follow-up, and no serious adverse events were reported. The change in the Autism Behavior Checklist total score did not differ between groups (p=0.44). Receptive language on the Psychoeducational Profile, Third Edition improved more in the intervention group (difference in change=2.38; 95% confidence interval, 0.19-4.57; p=0.03). Other subscales showed mixed findings, including problem behaviour favouring control. Regarding tolerability, while abdominal pain improved in the intervention group (p=0.01), reports of night waking (p=0.01) and looser stools (p=0.05) increased. The prespecified primary endpoint was not met. Exploratory findings suggested a signal in receptive language, alongside tolerability trade-offs. These results require confirmation in adequately powered trials with refined endpoint selection and structured safety monitoring.

papers.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
papers.abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

papers.title: Effect of Preoperative Intranasal Dexmedetomidine on Postoperative Myocardial Injury in Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the effects of preoperative intranasal dexmedetomidine on postoperative myocardial injury biomarkers in patients undergoing on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 70 patients undergoing on-pump CABG were assigned to receive intranasal dexmedetomidine (1 μg/kg) or saline 30 min before bedtime on the night before surgery and again 30 min before anesthesia induction. The primary outcome was serum high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) at 24 h after surgery. Secondary outcomes included perioperative cardiac biomarkers, preoperative sleep quality, postoperative delirium, and adverse events. For the prespecified primary outcome, hs-cTnT concentrations at 24 h after surgery were significantly lower in the dexmedetomidine group than in the control group (estimated marginal means, 170.29 vs 357.29 ng/L; P < 0.001). Postoperative creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB) concentrations were also lower in the dexmedetomidine group (all P < 0.05). N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide showed a significant group-by-time interaction (P = 0.030), although between-group differences at individual postoperative time points were not significant. The dexmedetomidine group had higher Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire scores (62 [60-64] vs 44 [41-50]; P < 0.001) and a lower incidence of postoperative delirium (14.3% vs 37.1%; P = 0.029). Adverse events, mechanical ventilation duration, and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay did not differ significantly between groups. In this single-center trial, two-dose preoperative intranasal dexmedetomidine was associated with lower postoperative hs-cTnT and CK-MB concentrations, better subjective preoperative sleep quality, and a lower observed incidence of postoperative delirium. These findings are preliminary and require confirmation in larger, adequately powered multicenter randomized trials to determine whether the biomarker reductions translate into clinically meaningful cardiovascular benefits. papers.title: Association of COVID-19 with neurodegenerative and neurological disorders in vaccinated and unvaccinated people
papers.abstract: Introduction: COVID-19 has been linked to neuropathology, neurological symptoms, and diagnoses of neurological illnesses. Evidence regarding the long-term impact of COVID-19 on neurodegenerative and neurological disorders is still limited. Methods: We investigated associations of COVID-19 with neurodegenerative and neurological disorders by vaccination status in both hospitalised patients and the general population in the largest and longest study to date. We used OpenSAFELY-TPP to access linked electronic health records from 18.3 million adults registered with English GPs. We defined three cohorts with up to 5.5 years follow-up: pre-vaccination (exposed to COVID-19 January 2020-June 2021), and vaccinated and unvaccinated (exposed June-December 2021). We estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) comparing the incidence of cognitive impairment and dementia after diagnosis of COVID-19 with before or without COVID-19. We also studied Parkinson's disease, restless leg syndrome, rapid eye movement sleep disorder, motor neuron disease, multiple sclerosis, and migraine. Results: Incidence of most outcomes was elevated during weeks 0-4 after COVID-19 (cognitive impairment/dementia aHRs; pre-vaccination: 4.02 (3.74-4.32)/5.05 (4.63-5.52), vaccinated: 2.24 (2.05-2.45)/2.05 (1.77-2.37), unvaccinated: 4.38 (3.45-5.55)/8.69 (6.13-12.32)). Incidence remained elevated up to 4 years after COVID-19, especially in those hospitalised with COVID-19 (cognitive impairment/dementia aHRs; pre-vaccination: 1.49 (1.35-1.64)/ 1.39 (1.21-1.60), vaccinated: 1.27 (1.04-1.54)/1.32 (1.02-1.71), unvaccinated: 1.55 (1.11-2.16)/1.48 (1.00-2.20)). Conclusion: Incidence of cognitive impairment and dementia were elevated shortly after COVID-19. Incidence of cognitive impairment remained elevated in the longer term, particularly among unvaccinated individuals and/or those hospitalised with COVID-19. These patients may require additional assessment during routine care to evaluate persistent or new cognitive concerns.

papers.title: Perimenopause and cardiometabolic risk: emerging evidence, therapeutic opportunities and unanswered questions.
papers.abstract: Perimenopause is increasingly recognized as a critical period for cardiometabolic health. During the years surrounding the final menstrual period, adverse changes in lipid profiles, insulin sensitivity, body composition and vascular function accelerate beyond those expected from aging alone, concurrent with the emergence and peak severity of menopause symptoms. Accumulating evidence suggests that vasomotor symptoms and sleep disturbance are associated with adverse cardiometabolic profiles and increased cardiovascular disease risk. Mechanistic data indicate that autonomic dysregulation, inflammation and neuroendocrine systems may represent shared pathways linking symptom burden and cardiometabolic dysfunction. Complementing these findings, prospective studies demonstrate that poor cardiovascular health and metabolic dysfunction may predict subsequent symptom development, suggesting that cardiometabolic health influences the menopause transition experience itself. Together, these findings support a model in which perimenopause represents a physiologic convergence point where symptom burden and cardiometabolic risk intersect, with implications for symptom management and primary prevention. However, major evidence gaps remain, including the absence of interventional studies during perimenopause and uncertainty regarding whether these relationships are causal or therapeutically modifiable. Future research should determine whether targeting cardiometabolic health during this window can improve both cardiovascular outcomes and the symptom experience of the menopause transition.

papers.title: Effects of far-infrared radiation on the nervous system and their potential.
papers.abstract: Far-infrared radiation (FIR; 3-1000 μm) is characterized by its strong tissue penetration and efficient heat conduction properties. Specifically, wavelengths within the range of 8-14 μm-often referred to as growth rays-are efficiently absorbed by living organisms, generating pronounced thermal effects. These wavelengths closely correspond to the natural vibrational wavelength of water molecules, thus enabling effective resonance and energy absorption. This property has led to their widespread use as a therapeutic tool in biomedical and healthcare applications. Because living organisms contain a substantial proportion of water, FIR can penetrate deeply into tissue, influencing various molecules through resonance with water molecules and modulating molecular mechanisms, thereby eliciting a range of physiological effects. The effects of FIR have been examined across diverse disciplines. The present review focuses on the effects of FIR on the nervous system. It compiles and discusses findings from previous studies that have used animal models of nervous system diseases to explore the direct effects of FIR on various aspects of the nervous system, including memory impairment, cognitive function, neural regeneration, sleep, anti-inflammatory effects, and stress relief.

papers.title: Respiratory function, allergic reactions and quality of life in individuals working in container-like confined spaces after the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to objectively evaluate the presence of allergic reactions and pulmonary function in individuals working in small container-like confined spaces in Malatya following the February 6, 2023, Kahramanmaraş-centered earthquakes, and to examine their associations with physical activity, sleep quality, grip strength, and quality of life. Given the well-established association between respiratory impairment and systemic effects on peripheral muscle strength, sleep architecture, and functional capacity, grip strength, sleep quality (PSQI), and physical activity (IPAQ-SF) were included as secondary outcomes to capture the broader functional burden of working in confined environments. This cross-sectional and descriptive study included 90 volunteers (aged 25-55 years) working in container-like spaces for at least two years. Pulmonary function was assessed using portable spirometry (FEV₁, FVC, FEV₁/FVC) according to the 2019 ATS/ERS guidelines, performed by trained physiotherapists. Physical activity was evaluated with IPAQ-SF, sleep quality with PSQI, quality of life with SF-36, and grip strength with a digital dynamometer. Multiple linear regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of respiratory function, controlling for age, smoking status, BMI, height, grip strength, and fatigue. Of 90 participants (92.2% male, mean age 39.0 ± 9.5 years), FEV₁% (68.9 ± 12.4) and FVC% (64.1 ± 11.3) were relatively low with a preserved FEV₁/FVC ratio (0.86 ± 0.06). mMRC dyspnea grade was significantly associated with FEV₁% and FVC% (p < 0.001). Multiple linear regression revealed that fatigue was a significant independent predictor of FEV₁% (β=-0.945, p = 0.044) and FEV₁ (L) (β=-0.053, p = 0.029) after controlling for confounders. Grip strength showed a positive trend with FEV₁% (β = 0.282, p = 0.082) and FVC% (β = 0.242, p = 0.092) that approached significance, consistent with the physiological link between respiratory and peripheral muscle function. The overall regression models were statistically significant (p < 0.01 for all models). Individuals working in small container-like spaces showed a tendency toward reduced ventilatory capacity without overt obstruction, and dyspnea was strongly associated with objective respiratory function loss. Fatigue emerged as an independent predictor of respiratory function. These findings highlight the importance of early screening strategies and further research with longitudinal designs, environmental measurements, and control groups to establish causal relationships.

papers.title: Self-Reported Cannabis Use, Pain and Mental Health in People With Inheritable Bleeding Disorders.
papers.abstract: Medical cannabis use has increased in the United States for managing symptoms such as pain, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and mood disorders. Self-report remains the primary method for documenting cannabis use. Little is known about cannabis use or perceived effectiveness among people with inheritable bleeding disorders (PWBD). Explore cannabis use patterns in PWBD who voluntarily participate in the Community Voices in Research (CVR) registry. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using self-reported CVR data, including demographics, diagnosis, cannabis use, and pain, depression, anxiety, resiliency/coping, and social support. Of 88 participants, 25 (28.4%) stated using cannabis for symptom management. Use was reported across hemophilia A, hemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, platelet disorders, and rare bleeding disorders. There were no statistically significant differences between groups for age, birth sex, and diagnosis. Participants most commonly cited pain, anxiety, sleep, and depression as reasons for use, with the highest perceived effectiveness (0-10 scale) for sleep (8.35), anxiety (7.06), and pain (6.36). Participants who reported cannabis use demonstrated higher anxiety scores and significantly higher opioid use compared to non-cannabis users. Cannabis use was relatively common among this small sample of PWBD. These patterns may reflect gaps in care. Higher anxiety scores and opioid use among participants who reported cannabis use support the need for proactive, non-judgmental assessment and comprehensive, patient-centered symptom management strategies in this population.

papers.title: The association between cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors in Austria and Slovakia: regression analyses based on the European Health Interview Survey (2019).
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) account for one in three deaths in the European Union. Slovakia has twice the rate of amenable mortality than neighboring Austria. This study aimed to examine the association between CVDs and risk factors and to describe similarities and differences in the observed patterns. Weighted 2019 European Health Interview Survey data were analyzed for adults aged ≥ 45 in Austria and Slovakia. Multivariable logistic regression analyses assessed associations between CVDs and its risk factors, adjusting for socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, and regions. The Austrian sample included 9,501 respondents and the SK sample 3,505. CVD prevalence was 8.8% in Austria and 15.3% in Slovakia. In both countries, sleep problems (Austria: OR: 1.90, 95% CI: 1.57-2.32; Slovakia: OR: 2.44, 95% CI: 1.95-3.04) were associated with reporting CVDs. In Austria, hypertension (OR: 1.88, 95% CI: 1.54-2.30), and diabetes (OR: 1.81, 95% CI: 1.42-2.31) were also associated with CVDs, as were diabetes (OR: 1.69, 95% CI: 1.31-2.20) and physical inactivity (OR: 1.65, 95% CI: 1.16-2.36) in Slovakia. Regional associations were more pronounced in Austria than in Slovakia. Although causality cannot be inferred, patterns in CVD prevalence and associated risk factors may support targeted national and regional prevention strategies.

papers.title: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent.
papers.abstract: A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

papers.title: Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Dose-Finding Study.
papers.abstract: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. papers.title: Longitudinal prediction of adolescent depression from environmental and polygenic risk scores.
papers.abstract: Understanding adolescent depression risk is vital for mitigating its long-term adverse effects. Though polygenic risk scores (PRS) explain increasing proportions of heritable risk, environmental risk remains challenging to quantify, hindering prediction. Existing prediction models often examine environmental risk in isolation, and vary in the number of predictors examined (between 8-800 + ), limiting generalisability. Here, we develop a model predicting adolescent depression symptoms (depRS) from a review of key environmental risk factors and assess depRS and PRS prediction of major depressive disorder (MDD) at 2-year follow-up. Using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (N = 9 797; 47% female), we generated PRS in European, African, American Admixed and East Asian ancestries from a recent trans-ancestry genome-wide study of MDD. We trained depRS to predict parent-reported depression symptoms at 2-year follow-up (age 11-13) from baseline predictors (age 9-11), using Elastic Net regression with 10-fold cross-validation for variable selection. The final depRS model included 12 predictors and explained 12.3% of overall variance. Parental depression, witnessing domestic violence, sleep duration and dieting emerged as top predictors of depression symptoms. depRS showed better-than-chance classification of parent- (AUC = 0.69 [0.66-0.73]) and youth self-reported MDD (AUC = 0.67 [0.64-0.71]), outperforming PRS classification of parent-reported MDD (AUC = 0.64 [0.60-0.68]). Combining depRS and PRS maximised accuracy for both outcomes (Parent AUC = 0.71 [0.68-0.75]; Youth AUC = 0.70 [0.66-0.73]). Though external validation of depRS across geographically and gender diverse cohorts is needed to assess generalisability, findings highlight sleep and dieting as potential targets for mitigating risk and demonstrate the utility of genetic scores in models predicting adolescent depression.

papers.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

papers.title: Avoiding Diagnostic Pitfalls in Facial Pain: A Case Report of Paroxysmal Hemicrania Initially Treated as Trigeminal Neuralgia.
papers.abstract: A 21-year-old man presented with a two-year history of recurrent, strictly unilateral left-sided pain in the upper maxillary and orbital regions, radiating to the temporal and occipital areas. Individual attacks lasted 20 to 30 minutes and occurred 10 to 20 times daily, on most days throughout the two-year period. He had been diagnosed elsewhere with trigeminal neuralgia and treated with carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily without benefit. He denied photophobia, phonophobia, and ipsilateral cranial autonomic features, but described prominent restlessness during attacks. No cutaneous or mucosal trigger could be identified, and neurological examination was normal. The attack duration, the reported high attack frequency, the absence of tactile triggers, and the restlessness were inconsistent with classical trigeminal neuralgia and raised suspicion of a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, including probable paroxysmal hemicrania. Carbamazepine was withdrawn, and an escalating oral indomethacin trial was initiated, reaching 225 mg daily and maintained at that dose for 14 consecutive days. A headache diary begun on the first day of the trial recorded headache on all 20 days, and the patient reported no improvement at any point. Because the phenotype fulfilled all but the indomethacin-response criterion, the diagnosis was recorded as probable paroxysmal hemicrania, while cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias remained in the differential diagnosis. Verapamil 240 mg daily was substituted on day 21. Headache days fell to 23 of 31 in the first month and 13 of 31 in the second, with the last 18 days of the second month free of headache. At telephone follow-up, the patient reported sustained resolution, with only mild headaches related to sleep deprivation that he considered distinct from his previous syndrome. He remains on verapamil. Whether verapamil produced the improvement cannot be established from a single uncontrolled case, as the drug was never withdrawn, and spontaneous remission remains possible. This case illustrates the clinical overlap between trigeminal neuralgia and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias and highlights the value of structured longitudinal symptom recording, ideally including individual attack count, duration, autonomic features, and triggers.

papers.title: Lived experiences and quality of life in people with severe, biologic-treated chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps: a hermeneutic phenomenological study.
papers.abstract: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) is an inflammatory disease that affects quality of life. Diagnostic delays, symptom recurrence, and treatment failure increase the uncertainty and frustration of those affected. The objective of this study was to retrospectively explore the lived experiences of people with severe, biologic-treated CRSwNP from the onset of symptoms through to the failure of both appropriate medical therapy and surgery, in relation to the impact of the disease on their quality of life. A qualitative study based on Gadamer's hermeneutics was conducted. Between April 2024 and April 2025, 16 adults with severe biologic-treated CRSwNP participated in the study. They were selected through purposive sampling in a single airway clinic. Medical history was taken, nasal examination was performed, and imaging tests were undertaken, followed by in-depth interviews. Data were interpreted following a Gadamerian hermeneutic-circle approach, operationalised through Fleming's method. Three main themes were developed: (1) the silent burden of symptoms and their impact on daily life; (2) the odyssey to obtain a diagnosis; and (3) the experience of treatment failure and the associated emotional strain. People with severe, biologic-treated CRSwNP experience communication and sleep difficulties, impaired sex life, discrimination and self-medication, which substantially deteriorates their quality of life. This is compounded by diagnostic uncertainty, the need for self-management, treatment failure, and the ongoing search for information. Family support has a meaningful impact on their biopsychosocial well-being. These findings illustrate how physical, emotional and social dimensions are intertwined throughout this disease trajectory.

papers.title: TruBlk™ Shilajit Resin Improves Sexual Function in Men with Erectile Dysfunction: A Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Multicenter Trial
papers.abstract: Erectile dysfunction and age-related testosterone decline are common and growing concerns among ageing men, yet current pharmacological options are constrained by tolerability, cost, and reluctance to start hormone-based therapy, leaving a real gap for safe, long-term alternatives. Shilajit, a resinous plant exudate long used in Ayurvedic medicine, is increasingly proposed to fill this gap with its bioactive constituents thought to confer adaptogenic, antioxidant, and androgen-modulating effects. However, clinical support for this use remains thin, with most existing trials small and conducted in healthy men rather than those with diagnosed erectile dysfunction. In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial (CTRI/2025/07/090919), 100 men aged 35-55 years with mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction (IIEF erectile function domain score 11-25) and symptoms suggestive of androgen deficiency were enrolled across two sites. Participants received 250 mg twice daily of standardised TruBlk Shilajit resin or matched placebo for 90 days. Primary endpoints, as registered, were change from baseline in IIEF total and domain scores, total and free testosterone and cortisol, and Hypogonadism Impact of Symptoms Questionnaire (HIS-Q) domain scores. Secondary endpoints included nitric oxide, Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), and Participant and Investigator Global Assessments. Semen parameters were assessed in a subset of participants. IIEF total score improved significantly more in the TruBlk group (+32.1% vs. +13.6%; d=0.67, p=0.005), with significant gains in four of the five domains, namely erectile function, orgasmic function, overall satisfaction, and intercourse satisfaction (d=0.52-0.61, p=0.011-0.044), while sexual desire showed a smaller, non-significant improvement (d=0.44, p=0.109). This was accompanied by significant increases in total testosterone (+46.1% vs. +10.0%; d=0.44, p=0.030) and free testosterone (+37.4% vs. +6.8%; d=0.41, p=0.048). HIS-Q symptom domains showed a similar pattern to IIEF, with Day 90 differences favouring TruBlk in three of five domains (sexual, energy, and sleep; d=-0.59 to -0.82, p<0.02), while cognition and mood showed smaller, non-significant differences (d=-0.46 to -0.49, p=0.06-0.10). Among secondary endpoints, fatigue fell substantially more with TruBlk than with placebo, with FSS scores decreasing by 51.8% vs. 27.4% from baseline, a large between-group effect at Day 90 (d=-1.13, p<0.0001). At Day 90, 56-58% of TruBlk participants were rated "Much" or "Very Much Improved" on global assessment, compared with 12-14% of placebo. Nitric oxide showed no significant between-group difference. In an exploratory semen-analysis subset (n=57), sperm concentration increased with TruBlk relative to placebo ({delta}=0.53, p<0.001), and in a subset of 40 participants assessed for motility, total motility ({delta}=0.63, p<0.001) and progressive motility (d=0.82, p=0.014) also improved. Ninety days of standardised TruBlk Shilajit resin improved erectile function and increased total and free testosterone in men with mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction, with improvement in several hypogonadism-related symptom domains, reduced fatigue and, in an exploratory subset, improved sperm concentration and motility. These results support standardised Shilajit resin as a promising intervention for sexual dysfunction in a clinically diagnosed population, meriting further clinical evaluation.
